verdict.summary:
# Approved Document B (Fire safety) Volume 1: Dwellings — sprinkler and common-stair trigger heights (England)

## 0. Answers at a glance

| Ask | Question | Answer | Status of the text relied on |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Governing document (constraint) | Approved Document B (Fire safety) Volume 1: Dwellings, 2019 edition incorporating the 2020 and 2022 amendments, **collated with the 2025, 2026 and 2029 amendments**, for use in England (GOV.UK consolidated PDF; Planning Portal: published July 2019, updated 2 March 2025) | Version identified, not a value ask — no numeric result |
| 2 | Top-storey height above ground above which blocks of flats should be fitted with a sprinkler system throughout | **11 m** — i.e. **more than 11 m** above ground level | In force (since 26 November 2020); unchanged by the 2022, 2025 and 2026 amendments |
| 3 | The same trigger height before the 2020 amendments | **30 m** — i.e. more than 30 m above ground level | Superseded text (2019 edition as published July 2019, and the 2006 edition as amended) |
| 4 | Top-storey height at which flats should be served by **more than one common stair** | **18 m** — ADB wording: a block of flats **with a storey 18 m or more in height** | In force (since 30 September 2026) |
| 5 | Date the changes introducing that multi-stair recommendation take effect | **30 September 2026**, for use in England | In force at the date of the source fetch (23 November 2026) |

All three figures are quoted directly from the published text; no interpolation has been done.

---

## 1. Version control (satisfying ask 1)

The answers are taken from the consolidated England text of **Approved Document B (Fire safety) Volume 1: Dwellings, 2019 edition incorporating the 2020 and 2022 amendments, collated with the 2025, 2026 and 2029 amendments** (GOV.UK asset `67d02309…`, SHA-256 prefix `b0b468a7`), cross-checked against:

- the 2019 edition **incorporating the 2020 amendments only** (asset `677fa136…`, `dde9a444`) — used for ask 3's before/after comparison;
- the 2019 edition **incorporating the 2020 and 2022 amendments** (asset `67d02386…`, `5ec1573c`) — used to confirm the 11 m figure survived the 2022 amendments;
- the **2026 amendments booklet** (asset `66d57a94…`, `852d8b8a`) — primary source for asks 4 and 5;
- the **May 2020 circular letter** (asset `924446…`, `d344799c`) — primary source for ask 3 and for the 2020 effective date.

Two scoping notes that matter for a defensible answer:

1. **The 2029 amendments are printed in the current PDF but are not in force.** They take effect **2 September 2029** for use in England. Ask 1's constraint expressly scopes the answer to "the 2020, 2022, 2025 and 2026 amendments", so the 2029 content is excluded. It should also be recorded that the 2026 booklet's own change log lists only two 2026 changes (multi-stair; evacuation-lift design provisions), and no fetched passage attributes any change to the 11 m sprinkler trigger or the 18 m stair trigger to the 2029 amendments.
2. **"Currently published" is date-sensitive.** At the source fetch date of 23 November 2026 the 2026 amendments (effective 30 September 2026) are in force, so answers 4 and 5 are live requirements of the current text, not future ones. Had the question been asked before 30 September 2026, ask 4 would have had no answer in ADB Vol 1 at all (single-stair design was the default), and ask 5 would have been a future date.

---

## 2. Ask 2 — Sprinkler trigger height in the current text: **more than 11 m**

**Source text (notes to Table B4, Minimum periods of fire resistance):**

> "2. Blocks of flats with a top storey more than 11m above ground level (see Diagram D6) should be fitted with a sprinkler system in accordance with Appendix E.
>
> NOTE: Sprinklers should be provided within the individual flats, they do not need to be provided in the common areas such as stairs, corridors or landings when these areas are fire sterile.
>
> 3. 'With sprinkler system' means that the building is fitted throughout with an automatic sprinkler system in accordance with Appendix E."

This wording is identical in the 2020-only, the 2020+2022 and the 2020+2022+2025+2026 collations — i.e. **the 11 m figure has not moved since 26 November 2020**, and the 2022, 2025 and 2026 amendments did not touch it.

**Engineering points a designer or building control body must apply to this answer:**

- **"Throughout" is defined, and is narrower than the plain English reading.** Note 3 defines "with sprinkler system" as fitted *throughout* in accordance with Appendix E, but the NOTE to note 2 records that sprinklers need be provided **within the individual flats** and not in common areas (stairs, corridors, landings) **where those areas are fire sterile**. "Fire sterile" means no fire load — a protected corridor used for resident storage, bin presentation or similar is not fire sterile, and the exemption does not then apply.
- **Standard.** Appendix E was not changed by the 2020 amendments; it recommends **BS 9251** for residential blocks of flats, or **BS EN 12845** for residential blocks of flats outside the scope of BS 9251.
- **Consequential effect on fire resistance.** The 2020 circular records that "Table B4 (Minimum periods of fire resistance) will also be amended when these changes take effect to reflect that a block of flats without a sprinkler system above 11 metres is not permitted if following the guidance in the Approved Document." A designer who departs from the 11 m sprinkler provision is therefore also departing from the Table B4 basis of the guidance and needs a fire-engineering justification covering fire resistance, not just the sprinkler omission.
- **Wording variance to be aware of.** The 2020 circular describes the trigger as "a top floor more than 11 metres above ground level" while ADB uses "top storey more than 11m". They are applied as the same trigger; ADB's "top storey" governs.
- **Boundary is exclusive.** "More than 11 m" — a block whose top storey is exactly 11.00 m does not trigger the note on a literal reading; 11.01 m does. Do not round down a design that lands on the boundary; resolve it with the building control body early.

---

## 3. Ask 3 — The trigger height before the 2020 amendments: **more than 30 m**

**Source text (May 2020 circular letter, 26 May 2020, "Summary of main changes"):**

> "**Sprinklers** — The amendments include a reduction in the height threshold for sprinklers in Purpose group 1a (residential (block of flats)) …"

and, in the "Main changes made by the 2020 amendments" page of the consolidated document:

> "a. **Sprinklers:** A reduction in the trigger height **from 30m to 11m**."

**Supporting corroboration that 30 m was the pre-2020 figure:** the same notes to Table B4 in the current text retain a 30 m trigger for non-residential uses — note 6: "Buildings within the 'office', 'shop and commercial', 'assembly and recreation', 'industrial' and 'storage and other non-residential' (except car parks for light vehicles) purpose groups (purpose groups 3 to 7(a)) require sprinklers where there is a top storey more than 30m above ground level." The 2020 amendment moved flats off the general 30 m figure and onto a dwelling-specific 11 m figure; the 30 m figure survives only for those non-residential purpose groups.

**Effective date of the change (for completeness, since ask 3 is a "before" value):** the 2020 amendments **take effect on 26 November 2020**, with transitional arrangements — they do not apply where a building notice or initial notice has been given, or full plans deposited, before that day and either the work started before 26 November 2020 or started before 29 January 2021. Blocks commenced under those arrangements legitimately remain on the 30 m basis.

**Do not confuse:** 30 m is no longer the flats trigger. Any answer that gives 30 m as the current figure for blocks of flats is reading the pre-2020 text or the purpose-group 3–7(a) note.

---

## 4. Ask 4 — More than one common stair: **a storey 18 m or more in height**

**Source text (2026 amendments booklet, "Summary of main changes" / "List of amendments"):**

> "The changes focus on the following fire safety provisions:
> a. **A new recommendation for more than one common stair to be provided in blocks of flats with a storey 18m or more in height.**
> b. Building design provisions to support the use of evacuation lifts in blocks of flats."

and in the consolidated Vol 1, "Changes made by the 2025, 2026 and 2029 amendments":

> "a. A new recommendation for more than one common stair to be provided in blocks of flats with a storey 18m or more in height."

**Where it lands in the document:** Section 3 (Means of escape – flats), subheading "Number of escape routes", where the booklet replaces paragraph 3.27 ("From the flat entrance door, a single escape route is acceptable in either of the following cases…") and adds the multi-stair provision alongside it. The booklet's extract does not show the paragraph number of the new multi-stair provision itself; cite it as **Section 3, "Number of escape routes"**, with the amendment booklet's summary page, until the paragraph number is read off the printed page.

**Engineering points:**

- **Wording differs from the sprinkler note.** The 2026 text says "**a storey** 18 m or more in height" — it does **not** say "top storey". For a block of flats the highest storey governs, so in practice it is the top storey that is measured, but do not quote it as "top storey more than 18 m"; the trigger is the presence of any storey at or above 18 m.
- **Boundary is inclusive**, unlike the sprinkler trigger. "18 m or more" means a building with a storey at exactly 18.00 m **does** attract the recommendation; a building with a storey at 17.9 m does not.
- **Interaction with ask 2.** Any block caught by the 18 m stair recommendation is necessarily more than 11 m, so from 30 September 2026 a block with a storey at 18 m or above attracts **both** the throughout-sprinkler provision (Table B4 note 2) **and** the two-common-stair recommendation. A worked boundary set:
  - top storey 10.5 m → no sprinklers, single stair acceptable;
  - top storey 11.0 m → literal reading: no sprinkler requirement; single stair acceptable;
  - top storey 12.0 m → sprinklers required; single stair acceptable (subject to paragraph 3.27 conditions and protected lobby/corridor provisions);
  - top storey 18.0 m → sprinklers required **and** more than one common stair recommended.
- **It is guidance, not a statutory requirement in terms.** Like all ADB provisions it is one way of satisfying the Building Regulations; the recommendation is the deemed-to-satisfy route. Departure needs an equivalent-standard justification accepted by the building control body.
- **Companion change.** The same 2026 amendments introduce building design provisions supporting evacuation lifts in blocks of flats; a two-stair layout and evacuation-lift design should be developed together.

---

## 5. Ask 5 — Effective date: **30 September 2026**

**Source text (2026 amendments booklet, introduction):**

> "The changes highlighted in this amendment booklet **take effect on 30 September 2026 for use in England**. The 2019 edition incorporating the 2020, 2022 and 2025 amendments will continue to apply …"

and in the consolidated Vol 1:

> "**2026 amendments** — The 2026 amendments take effect on **30 September 2026** for use in England. The 2019 edition incorporating the 2020, 2022 and 2025 amendments will continue to apply where a building notice or an initial notice has been given to, or a building control approval application with full plans made to, the relevant authority before 30 September 2026 and either the building work to which it relates:
> a. has started and is sufficiently progressed before that day; or
> b. is started and is sufficiently progressed within the period of 18 months beginning on that day."

**Transitional effect — this is the point most often got wrong:**

- The **implementation date is 30 September 2026**, not the booklet's publication date (the booklet records "First published March 2024; Updated September 2024; Taking effect on 30 September 2026"). A building control application made in 2024/2025 does not bring the multi-stair recommendation forward; it is the notice/deposit date plus progress test that decides.
- Where a building notice, initial notice or full-plans application was made **before 30 September 2026** and the work either **started and is sufficiently progressed before that day**, or **is started and sufficiently progressed within the 18 months beginning on that day (i.e. by 30 March 2028)**, the pre-2026 text (2019 edition incorporating the 2020, 2022 and 2025 amendments) continues to apply — single-stair design remains available on that route.
- The same structure applies to the 2025 amendments, which **take effect on 2 March 2025** for use in England (their listed changes — including new sprinkler provisions for care homes — do not alter the flats trigger in ask 2).

---

## 6. Threshold disambiguation table (all figures appearing in ADB Vol 1 that are commonly confused)

| Height | Provision | Wording / trigger | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| **11 m** | **Sprinklers throughout, blocks of flats** | **more than 11 m** (exclusive) | Table B4 note 2 (2020 amendments) |
| 11 m | Wayfinding signage for the fire service | storeys over 11 m | 2020 amendments |
| 11 m | Secure information box | storeys over 11 m | 2022 amendments |
| 11 m | External wall / Section 10 provisions for residential (purpose groups 1 and 2) | storey 11 m or more | 2022 amendments |
| 18 m | Evacuation alert systems | storeys over 18 m | 2022 amendments |
| **18 m** | **More than one common stair, blocks of flats** | **a storey 18 m or more** (inclusive) | **2026 amendments, effective 30 September 2026** |
| 18 m | "Very large" dwellinghouses outside the scope of dwellinghouse guidance | more than 18 m (or 10 m deep basement) | Table B4 note 4 |
| 30 m | Sprinklers, purpose groups 3–7(a) (non-residential) | more than 30 m | Table B4 note 6 |
| **30 m** | **Pre-2020 sprinkler trigger for flats (superseded)** | **more than 30 m** | **2019 edition before the 2020 amendments** |

---

## 7. Verification trail and residual uncertainty

**Verified by direct quotation:** the 11 m sprinkler trigger (three separate collations, identical wording); the 30 m pre-2020 figure (2020 circular + change-log page, "from 30m to 11m"); the 18 m multi-stair figure (2026 booklet + consolidated change log, identical wording); the 30 September 2026 effective date (2026 booklet introduction + consolidated change log, identical wording). No figure in this answer contradicts a limit stated elsewhere in this answer: 18 m > 11 m, so the stated interaction (both provisions apply at ≥18 m) is consistent; the exclusive/inclusive distinction is stated explicitly wherever the boundary is discussed.

**Residual points a reviewer should close on the printed page (they do not change the four values, but they do change how they are cited):**

1. **Diagram D6 datum.** Table B4 note 2 refers to Diagram D6 for the measurement of "top storey … above ground level". The fetched extracts do not reproduce the diagram. The convention applied in practice is measurement from ground level to the **top of the floor of the top storey** of the topmost storey; confirm against Diagram D6 in the copy held before applying the answer to a design sitting on the boundary (11.0 m / 18.0 m).
2. **Paragraph number of the multi-stair provision.** The 2026 booklet replaces paragraph 3.27 and introduces the subheading "Number of escape routes"; the new provision's own paragraph number is not visible in the extract. Cite Section 3 plus the booklet until confirmed.
3. **2029 amendments.** Present in the current PDF but not in force until 2 September 2029 and outside ask 1's stated scope. If the question is re-run after that date, re-check whether any 2029 change touches the 11 m or 18 m triggers before reusing these answers.
4. **Wales/Scotland/Northern Ireland.** These answers are England-only, as ask 1 requires. The Welsh ADB Vol 1 and the Scottish Technical Handbooks have different triggers and must not be substituted.

---

## 8. One-line answers for issue to a design team

- Sprinklers throughout: blocks of flats with a **top storey more than 11 m** above ground level (Table B4 note 2; sprinklers within flats, common areas only where not fire sterile; BS 9251 / BS EN 12845 per Appendix E).
- Before the 2020 amendments that figure was **more than 30 m** (reduced to 11 m by the 2020 amendments, effective **26 November 2020**, with transitional relief for work commenced under the pre-2020 text).
- More than one common stair: blocks of flats **with a storey 18 m or more in height**, recommended by the 2026 amendments, **taking effect 30 September 2026** for use in England (transitional relief for applications made before that date and sufficiently progressed before it, or started and sufficiently progressed by 30 March 2028).

verdict.summary:
METROLOGY NOTE — Rydberg constant R_infinity: CODATA 2022 recommended value, its standard uncertainty, and the superseded CODATA 2018 value.

1. QUANTITY DEFINITION (identity check, done first)
The quantity requested is the Rydberg constant R_infinity itself, in SI inverse metres (m^-1). It is NOT: the Rydberg frequency cR_infinity (3.289 841 960 2500(36) x 10^15 Hz in 2022), the Rydberg energy hcR_infinity (13.605 693 122 990(15) eV in 2022), or the Rydberg constant times hc in J. All three appear adjacent to R_infinity on the same NIST chart and are a common transcription error. The three numbers below are the constant R_infinity only.
Unit convention, as stated by NIST on the value page footnote and on the wall charts: 'The full description of unit m^-1 is cycles or periods per meter.' This is a phase/angle convention, not an uncertainty or a correction; no numerical adjustment is applied. Values are quoted in the CODATA convention, k = 1 (one standard uncertainty), not expanded uncertainty.

2. CODATA 2022 RECOMMENDED VALUE (answers asks 1 and 2)
Source A — NIST CODATA value page for the Rydberg constant, https://physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/cuu/Value?ryd, footer 'Source: 2022 CODATA recommended values' (Web Version 9.0, 9 May 2024, Tiesinga, Mohr, Newell & Taylor, 'The 2022 CODATA Recommended Values of the Fundamental Physical Constants'):
  Numerical value:            10 973 731.568 157   m^-1
  Standard uncertainty:              0.000 012   m^-1
  Relative standard uncertainty:     1.1 x 10^-12
  Concise form:               10 973 731.568 157(12) m^-1
Source B — NIST SP 961 wall chart 'CODATA RECOMMENDED VALUES OF THE FUNDAMENTAL PHYSICAL CONSTANTS: 2022', https://pml.nist.gov/cuu/pdf/wall_2022.pdf (May 2024), Atomic and Nuclear / General block:
  Rydberg constant  R_infinity  10 973 731.568 157(12)  [m^-1]
Two independent NIST-published surfaces agree digit-for-digit, so no reconciliation is required.

ANSWER, ask 1: R_infinity (2022 CODATA) = 10 973 731.568 157 m^-1 = 1.097 373 156 815 7 x 10^7 m^-1.
ANSWER, ask 2: u(R_infinity) = 0.000 012 m^-1 = 1.2 x 10^-5 m^-1 (one standard uncertainty), equivalently the parenthetical form 10 973 731.568 157(12) m^-1, where (12) is the uncertainty in the last two digits of the mantissa. Relative standard uncertainty 1.1 x 10^-12.

3. CODATA 2018 VALUE THAT WAS REPLACED (answers ask 3)
Source C — NIST SP 961 wall chart 'CODATA RECOMMENDED VALUES OF THE FUNDAMENTAL PHYSICAL CONSTANTS: 2018', https://physics.nist.gov/cuu/pdf/wall_2018.pdf (May 2019):
  Rydberg constant  R_infinity  10 973 731.568 160(21)  [m^-1]
Source D — 2018 CODATA adjustment, extensive listing, https://pml.nist.gov/cuu/pdf/all_2018.pdf, 'Fundamental Physical Constants — Extensive Listing', General block:
  Rydberg constant  R_infinity  10 973 731.568 160(21)  [m^-1]   relative std. uncert. 1.9 x 10^-12
  (same page: Rydberg frequency 3.289 841 960 2508(64) x 10^15 Hz; hcR_infinity 2.179 872 361 1035(42) x 10^-18 J / 13.605 693 122 994(26) eV — listed only to confirm identity, not part of the answer.)
Source E — NIST CODATA version-history page, https://physics.nist.gov/cuu/Reference/versioncon.shtml, Version 9.0 (9 May 2024): 'Values updated to the 2022 CODATA recommended values. The 2022 values replace the previously recommended 2018 CODATA values, which are available in archived tables.' This is the documentary warrant that 2018 is precisely the set that 2022 superseded — i.e. that 2018 is 'the value it replaced'.

ANSWER, ask 3: R_infinity (2018 CODATA) = 10 973 731.568 160 m^-1 = 1.097 373 156 816 0 x 10^7 m^-1, with u = 0.000 021 m^-1 (relative 1.9 x 10^-12), parenthetical form 10 973 731.568 160(21) m^-1. The 2018 standard uncertainty is supplied as provenance; the ask requested only the value.

4. CONSISTENCY / INTERNAL AUDIT OF THE THREE NUMBERS ABOVE
(a) Parenthesis decoding. 2022: mantissa written to 10^-6 m^-1, (12) -> u = 12 x 10^-6 = 0.000 012 m^-1. 2018: (21) -> u = 21 x 10^-6 = 0.000 021 m^-1. Both agree with the explicitly printed uncertainties on the respective value/extensive-listing pages.
(b) Relative uncertainty recomputation. 2022: 1.2e-5 / 1.0973731568157e7 = 1.0935e-12 -> 1.1e-12 as published. 2018: 2.1e-5 / 1.0973731568160e7 = 1.9136e-12 -> 1.9e-12 as published. No contradiction between absolute and relative statements.
(c) Shift between adjustments. Delta = 10 973 731.568 160 - 10 973 731.568 157 = 0.000 003 m^-1 = 3 x 10^-6 m^-1 (2022 lower than 2018). Combined 1-sigma = sqrt(12^2 + 21^2) x 10^-6 = 24.19 x 10^-6 m^-1. Delta/combined = 0.124 sigma. Therefore the note must NOT describe this as a significant shift in the central value; the defensible statement is that the central value moved by 3 in the last published digit (0.12 combined sigma, not significant) while the standard uncertainty improved by a factor 21/12 = 1.75 (consistent with the published relative uncertainties, 1.9e-12 -> 1.1e-12, ratio 1.73). This is the check that guards against a summary that overstates the change.
(d) Unit and magnitude sanity. R_infinity = alpha^2 m_e c / 2h; using 2022 alpha^-1 = 137.035 999 177(21) and m_e = 9.109 383 7139(28) x 10^-31 kg reproduces 1.0973 x 10^7 m^-1 to the stated digits. Magnitude ~1.1 x 10^7 m^-1 (i.e. ~91.1 nm photon for the Lyman limit) is the expected order; a value off by 10^2 or 10^7 would signal a cm^-1 or per-angstrom transcription.
(e) No figure in this note exceeds or contradicts any bound, threshold, or uncertainty stated elsewhere in the note. The three reported numbers are the two central values and one uncertainty, all at full CODATA precision.

5. HOW TO QUOTE / ROUND (guidance for downstream use)
- Full precision, as published: R_infinity = 10 973 731.568 157(12) m^-1 (2022); 10 973 731.568 160(21) m^-1 (2018).
- If fewer digits are needed, truncate the mantissa and the parenthetical together, e.g. 10 973 731.5682(1) m^-1 is NOT acceptable (uncertainty rounded to 1 digit while mantissa keeps 4 decimals); acceptable forms are 10 973 731.568 16(13) m^-1 (uncertainty rounded up, conservative) or 10 973 731.568 157(12) m^-1 as published.
- State k = 1 (standard, not expanded). CODATA does not publish a coverage factor for these tables; if a 95% interval is needed, do not multiply by 1.96 blindly without noting the approximation, since the adjustment is a least-squares fit with correlations.
- Cite as: Eite Tiesinga, Peter J. Mohr, David B. Newell, and Barry N. Taylor (2024), 'The 2022 CODATA Recommended Values of the Fundamental Physical Constants' (Web Version 9.0), Database developed by J. Baker, M. Douma, and S. Kotochigova, available at https://physics.nist.gov/constants, NIST, Gaithersburg, MD 20899.

6. PROVENANCE OF EACH FIGURE
2022 central value and u: NIST CUU value page (Value?ryd) + NIST SP 961 wall chart 2022. 2018 central value and u: NIST SP 961 wall chart 2018 + 2018 CODATA extensive listing. Succession (2018 replaced by 2022): NIST CODATA version-history page. All are NIST-published; no third-party mirror, textbook, or recalled-from-memory figure was used.

for the various classes. The rationale for specific requirements is stated where possible.

with the requirements of the strictest applicable class or in some cases the strictest requirements

a piece of electronic equipment powered from the system power supply. It would require Class R

quotes.whole:
B.3.1 Design Parameters
Since a single bond may serve multiple purposes, electrical bonding is performed in accordance
with the requirements of the strictest applicable class or in some cases the strictest requirements
from more than one class. An example of electrical bonding for more than one purpose would be
a piece of electronic equipment powered from the system power supply. It would require Class R
bonding for RF and Class H bonding for fault current protection. Since both classes are
applicable, the bond should be low inductance with no more than 2.5 milliohms dc resistance for
Class R, and the contact area should be adequate to carry the maximum fault current that could
occur for Class H.
A nose cone should meet the lightning and static charge requirements. The Class L requirement
calls for low inductance, low resistance, and adequate area to carry lightning current. Since the
bond requirement for static charge is only moderately low resistance, the lightning bond will be
sufficient for both.
The only requirement for conductive tubing carrying fluid will be to meet the Class S
requirement. An electrical bond to basic structure of 1.0 ohm or less will be adequate.

quotes.whole:
B.3.1 Design Parameters
Since a single bond may serve multiple purposes, electrical bonding is performed in accordance
with the requirements of the strictest applicable class or in some cases the strictest requirements
from more than one class. An example of electrical bonding for more than one purpose would be
a piece of electronic equipment powered from the system power supply. It would require Class R
bonding for RF and Class H bonding for fault current protection. Since both classes are
applicable, the bond should be low inductance with no more than 2.5 milliohms dc resistance for
Class R, and the contact area should be adequate to carry the maximum fault current that could
occur for Class H.
A nose cone should meet the lightning and static charge requirements. The Class L requirement
calls for low inductance, low resistance, and adequate area to carry lightning current. Since the
bond requirement for static charge is only moderately low resistance, the lightning bond will be
sufficient for both.
The only requirement for conductive tubing carrying fluid will be to meet the Class S
requirement. An electrical bond to basic structure of 1.0 ohm or less will be adequate.

verdict.summary:
# Class R (EMI/RF) Bond Requirement — NASA-STD-4003A, w/Change 1

## 1. Bottom line

**There is no maximum RF impedance in ohms at a stated frequency for a Class R bond in NASA-STD-4003A.** The standard does not contain one, at any frequency. The question as asked has a false premise, and any answer of the form "X ohms at Y MHz per NASA-STD-4003A" is not traceable to the standard.

What the standard *actually* requires for Class R is a **DC bond resistance of 2.5 milliohms (0.0025 Ω) or less across each bonding joint, with low inductance**, achieved preferentially by **direct metal-to-metal contact**, with **no jumpers** and a short, wide strap only as a last resort.

## 2. The Class R requirement, as written

Source: NASA-STD-4003A w/Change 1, Table 1, "Summary of Electrical Bonding Classes" (p. 15 of 47), and Appendix B.3.1, "Design Parameters." Retrieved from the NASA Technical Standards System (standards.nasa.gov), document revalidated 03/13/2026.

**Table 1, Class R column — verbatim:**

| Table 1 field | Class R entry |
|---|---|
| BOND REQMT. | "Requires low RF impedance at high frequency. Direct contact preferred. No jumpers. Short, wide strap may be used as last resort." |
| DC BOND RESISTANCE REQMT. | "Bonding resistance requirement, 2.5 milliohms or less. Low inductance required." |
| FREQ. REQMT. | High |
| CURRENT REQMT. | Low |

**Appendix B.3.1 — verbatim, in the worked example of a box that needs both Class R and Class H:**

> "It would require Class R bonding for RF and Class H bonding for fault current protection. Since both classes are applicable, the bond should be low inductance with no more than 2.5 milliohms dc resistance for Class R, and the contact area should be adequate to carry the maximum fault current that could occur for Class H."

**Independent corroboration — MSFC-HDBK-3697 (Electrical Bonding Design Guide Handbook, Baseline, 24 Mar 2014), §4.3:**

> "Historically, the Class R bond has been associated with a 2.5 mohm resistance across each bonding joint. The resistance of a bond joint does not change with frequency. Unfortunately, there are no purely resistive joints in the real world. All circuits, including bonding paths, contain elements of capacitance and inductance that have reactances that vary with frequency."

That handbook sentence is the crux: the 4003A Class R number is a **DC resistance**, and it is frequency-invariant by definition. The standard compensates for the frequency dependence of a real joint not with an impedance number but with a **qualitative design mandate** — low inductance, direct contact, no jumpers, short wide strap as last resort. The "FREQ. REQMT. = High" entry in Table 1 is a classification of the bond's *purpose* (it must work at high frequency), not a numeric impedance at a stated frequency.

## 3. Why there is no "ohms at a stated frequency" figure

- The standard's compliance metric for Class R is a **4-wire DC resistance measurement**, not a network-analyzer impedance measurement. No test frequency, no test fixture, and no impedance magnitude limit are defined for Class R anywhere in 4003A.
- A DC resistance limit is deliberately used because it is a *producibility and workmanship* screen (surface finish, faying-surface contact area, fastener torque, corrosion control), while the RF performance is controlled by the **inductance** of the path — which is controlled by geometry (direct contact, short/wide strap, no pigtails), not by a resistance number.
- Consequently, if a program needs an actual RF impedance figure at a frequency, it does not come from 4003A. It comes from one of: (a) program-level tailoring of 4003A, (b) a derived requirement in the EMI/EMC control plan, (c) MIL-STD-464 (system-level), or (d) a transfer-impedance specification on a shield/connector. Do not cite 4003A for such a number.

## 4. Non-normative illustration (NOT a NASA-STD-4003A requirement)

To show a reviewer why the standard refuses to state a single-frequency number, take a joint that just meets the limit, R = 2.5 mΩ, with a typical short direct-contact inductance of L = 10 nH:

|Z| = sqrt(R² + (2πfL)²)

- f = 1 MHz: |Z| ≈ 63 mΩ
- f = 10 MHz: |Z| ≈ 0.63 Ω
- f = 100 MHz: |Z| ≈ 6.3 Ω

The DC-compliant joint is already 250× its DC resistance at 1 MHz and 2500× at 100 MHz. This is exactly why the Class R requirement is written as "low inductance, direct contact, no jumpers" — the geometry clause, not a number, is what delivers the RF performance. Treat these figures as engineering context only; they are not a compliance limit and must not be cited as one.

## 5. Verification procedure the designer should actually specify

For each Class R joint on the drawing/ATP:

1. **Method:** 4-wire (Kelvin) DC resistance measurement with a calibrated milliohmmeter. Do not use a 2-wire DMM; lead and probe resistance swamps a 2.5 mΩ limit.
2. **Limit:** ≤ 2.5 mΩ **across each bonding joint** — per joint, not end-to-end. A box-to-structure path through three joints is three joints at 2.5 mΩ each, not one 2.5 mΩ path. This is the single most common misapplication of the Class R number.
3. **Probe placement:** probe on bare, clean metal immediately either side of the joint interface; probe pressure and tip geometry fixed and recorded. Subtract probe/lead zero (short the tips on the same material).
4. **Condition:** measure in the as-built, as-finished configuration (after plating/coating and torque-up), and record surface finish and torque value on the record.
5. **Design compliance (checked by inspection, not by meter):** direct metal-to-metal contact present; no jumper used; if a strap is used, it is short and wide (low L/D ratio, flat braid or sheet, not round wire with long pigtails); fasteners torqued to drawing; faying surfaces are conductive finishes.
6. **Drawing note, suggested wording:** "THE RESISTANCE ACROSS THIS JOINT SHALL BE LESS THAN 2.5 MILLIOHMS TO MEET THE ELECTRICAL BOND REQUIREMENTS OF NASA-STD-4003, CLASS R. DIRECT METAL-TO-METAL CONTACT REQUIRED; NO JUMPERS." (This note form follows the MSFC-HDBK-3697 §6.2 example notes.)

## 6. Design guidance that actually drives Class R success

- **Finish:** bare/chem-film (MIL-DTL-5541 Type II or III, Class 3, conductive) aluminum faying surfaces; no anodize, no paint, no primer in the bond path. Mask bond areas before finishing.
- **Geometry:** maximize contact area and minimize loop length; the inductance, not the resistance, is what fails EMC tests.
- **Jumpers:** the standard says no jumpers for Class R. Where a jumper is unavoidable (assembly/serviceability), use flat braid, as short and wide as physically possible, bonded at both ends with the same 2.5 mΩ per-joint limit at each end — and treat it as a deviation with rationale.
- **Corrosion:** avoid dissimilar-metal couples (e.g., aluminum-to-CFRP, aluminum-to-stainless) without a compatible conductive interface; a joint that passes at build can exceed 2.5 mΩ after humidity/temperature cycling. Specify the resistance check after environmental exposure for critical bonds.
- **Multi-class joints:** if the joint is also Class H (fault current), the strictest requirement of each class applies simultaneously — 2.5 mΩ DC *and* low inductance for Class R, plus adequate contact area to carry the Class H fault current (per Appendix B.3.1).

## 7. Citation block for the design record

- NASA-STD-4003A w/Change 1, *Electrical Bonding for NASA Launch Vehicles, Spacecraft, Payloads, and Flight Equipment*, approved for public release, distribution unlimited; revalidated 03/13/2026.
  - Table 1, Summary of Electrical Bonding Classes, p. 15 of 47 — Class R row.
  - §4.1, Electrical Bonding ([EBR 5], multiple-purpose bonds).
  - Appendix B.3.1, Design Parameters — "no more than 2.5 milliohms dc resistance for Class R." (Appendix A.3.1 in the pre-Change-1 printing.)
- MSFC-HDBK-3697, *Electrical Bonding Design Guide Handbook*, Baseline, 24 Mar 2014, §4.3 (RF/Class R bonding) and §6.2 (drawing note examples).

## 8. What was and was not verified against the controlled document

Verified from retrieved primary text: the Class R row of Table 1, the FREQ./CURRENT classification entries, and the Appendix B.3.1 sentence stating 2.5 mΩ DC for Class R. Also verified: the document revision and revalidation date, and that NASA-STD-4003A supersedes the base NASA-STD-4003.

Not verified, and to be confirmed against the controlled copy before quoting in a CDR package: the exact **EBR paragraph number** in Section 4 that carries the Class R resistance requirement itself (the retrieved excerpts contained §4.1 and [EBR 5] but not the Class R-specific EBR line). The value (2.5 mΩ) is not in doubt — it is corroborated in two independent places in the standard and again in the MSFC handbook — but the paragraph citation should be filled in from the controlled copy rather than from memory.

## 9. Direct answer to the designer

You cannot get an "ohms at a frequency" number out of 4003A, because the standard does not define one. Design and verify to **2.5 mΩ DC per joint with a low-inductance, direct-contact geometry**, and if your program genuinely needs an RF impedance limit at a frequency, raise it as a program-tailored or derived requirement and state its source explicitly — do not attribute it to NASA-STD-4003A.

NTDE
National Tidal Datum Epoch
The National Tidal Datum Epoch (NTDE) is a 19-year time period established by the National Ocean Service for collecting observations on water levels and calculating tidal datum values (e.g. mean sea level, mean lower low water). The NTDE needs to be regularly revised to account for long-term effects of land movement, sea level rise, and changes in tidal constituents. Tidal datums and their data are used to generate products and services necessary for safe navigation, coastal hazard mitigation, ecosystem research, coastal engineering, and marine boundary demarcations.
The NTDE Update: New Tidal Datums are Coming!
NOAA currently utilizes the 1983-2001 National Tidal Datum Epoch. This epoch is now undergoing revision and will be replaced by the fifth iteration of the NTDE. Measurements for the update will be based on water level data spanning the years 2002-2020. Once all data has been collected, NOAA will review, analyze, and generate revised datums. The current proposed release date for new NTDE products is in 2029.

quotes.whole:
Datum Updates
Tide and water level datums are standard elevations used to reference water level heights and depths. Each type of datum represents a unique phase or behavior of the water along the coast or in the Great Lakes. CO-OPS and its partners are currently in the midst of two large-scale datum updates for the National Tidal Datum Epoch (NTDE) and the International Great Lakes Datum (IGLD).
To obtain datums for a specific location, please visit the CO-OPS Datums Station Selection web pages.
National Tidal Datum Epoch
The NTDE is a specific 19-year reference period over which water level observations are taken to determine Mean Sea Level and other tidal datums (e.g., Mean Lower Low Water). The NTDE has historically been updated every 20-25 years.
International Great Lakes Datum
The IGLD is a common reference system used to measure water level heights throughout the Great Lakes, their connecting waterways, and the St. Lawrence River System. The IGLD is updated every 25-30 years.

## Findings (NOAA CO-OPS, verbatim)

**Source of record:** NOAA CO-OPS, National Tidal Datum Epoch page — https://www.tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datum-updates/ntde/ (fetched 2026-11-23T11:56:46Z, sha256 4fa508e48279…). Corroborating source: CO-OPS Tidal Analysis Datum Calculator — https://access.co-ops.nos.noaa.gov/datumcalc/ (fetched 2026-11-23T11:56:47Z, sha256 2999991682c4…). A third corroboration: CO-OPS ArcGIS `Datums_Stations` iteminfo (mapservices.weather.noaa.gov).

### Ask 1 — constraint: authority is NOAA CO-OPS
All three values below are taken from NOAA Center for Operational Oceanographic Products and Services (CO-OPS) pages on tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov and access.co-ops.nos.noaa.gov — the office that establishes and publishes U.S. tidal datums. No third-party summary, news article, or secondary source was used.

### Ask 2 — Current 19-year NTDE: **1983–2001**
NTDE page, verbatim:

> "NOAA currently utilizes the 1983-2001 National Tidal Datum Epoch. This epoch is now undergoing revision and will be replaced by the fifth iteration of the NTDE."

Corroboration — Datum Calculator epoch selector offers `Present (1983 - 2001)`; the CO-OPS `Datums_Stations` layer description states "The 'Present Epoch' is from 1983-2001 and includes the latest datums available."

### Ask 3 — Fifth (replacement) epoch water-level data years: **2002–2020**
NTDE page, verbatim:

> "Measurements for the update will be based on water level data spanning the years 2002-2020."

Corroboration — Datum Calculator offers a `New (2002 - 2020)` epoch, and its warning dialog reads: "You have requested to compute datums for your data relative to the 2002-2020 National Tidal Datum Epoch, which has not yet been released by NOAA."

### Ask 4 — Proposed release year for new-epoch products: **2029**
NTDE page, verbatim:

> "The current proposed release date for new NTDE products is in 2029."

Corroboration — Datum Calculator warning: preliminary control datums "may be different from those that are planned to be officially released in early 2029."

## Verification / internal consistency
- The NTDE is defined on the same page as "a 19-year time period established by the National Ocean Service for collecting observations on water levels and calculating tidal datum values."
- 1983–2001 inclusive = 2001 − 1983 + 1 = **19 years** ✓
- 2002–2020 inclusive = 2020 − 2002 + 1 = **19 years** ✓
- The fifth epoch begins the calendar year immediately after the present epoch closes (2001 → 2002): no gap, no overlap. ✓
- Both the prose page and the calculator independently give 2029, so the release year is not an artifact of a single stale page.

## Caveats a downstream user should carry
1. **2029 is a stated target, not a contractual commitment.** Both NOAA pages call it "proposed" / "planned"; it is subject to revision. Treat it as the currently published proposal, which is exactly what the question asks.
2. **The 2002–2020 epoch is not yet official.** NOAA's own calculator labels datums computed on it "Preliminary, unofficial… for planning purposes only." Official U.S. tidal datums (on nautical charts, tide tables, and datum pages) remain on 1983–2001 until the new epoch is released.
3. **Currency of the answer:** values are as published on the pages fetched 2026-11-23. NOAA CO-OPS pages can lag announcements; the two-source agreement above reduces, but does not eliminate, that risk. If a later check shows a revised release year, only Ask 4 changes — the epoch years (1983–2001 present; 2002–2020 replacement) are fixed by the observation record and are stable.

## Answer in one line
NOAA CO-OPS currently bases official U.S. tidal datums on the **1983–2001** National Tidal Datum Epoch; the replacement fifth epoch will use water-level data spanning **2002–2020**; NOAA currently proposes releasing products based on the new epoch in **2029**.

verdict.summary:
TRAFFIC ENGINEERING ANSWER — MUTCD pedestrian interval timing (11th Ed., Dec. 2023, incl. Rev. 1) vs. 2009 MUTCD

1. ANSWERS

| # | Question | Answer | Authority |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Minimum buffer interval (steady UPRAISED HAND) after the pedestrian change interval, before release of a conflicting vehicular movement | 2 seconds (minimum; a floor, not a target) | MUTCD 11th Ed., §4I.06, ¶04 (Standard) |
| 2 | Default walking speed for sizing pedestrian clearance time | 3.5 ft/s (≈1.07 m/s), reduced where slower pedestrians or wheelchair users routinely use the crosswalk | MUTCD 11th Ed., §4I.06, ¶¶07–16 with ¶10 (Guidance) establishing 3.5 ft/s as the baseline |
| 3 | Buffer-interval minimum in the 2009 MUTCD | 3 seconds | MUTCD 2009, §4E.06, ¶3 (Standard) — same requirement, older section numbering |

Net change 2009 → 11th Ed.: the buffer minimum was reduced from 3 s to 2 s, while simultaneously being made unconditional (the buffer must now always be provided and displayed, not merely before a conflicting release).

2. GOVERNING TEXT — 11th EDITION, §4I.06 (verbatim, Standard ¶04)

"A pedestrian change interval consisting of a flashing UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall begin immediately following the WALKING PERSON (symbolizing WALK) signal indication. Following the pedestrian change interval, a buffer interval consisting of a steady UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall be displayed for at least 2 seconds prior to the release of any conflicting vehicular movement. The sum of the time of the pedestrian change interval and the buffer interval shall not be less than the calculated pedestrian clearance time (see Paragraphs 7 through 16 of this Section). The buffer interval shall not begin later than the beginning of the red clearance interval, if used."

Three binding constraints are packed into that paragraph and all three must be satisfied simultaneously by any timing plan:
(a) buffer ≥ 2.0 s, ending no earlier than the instant the conflicting vehicular movement is released;
(b) (pedestrian change interval) + (buffer) ≥ calculated pedestrian clearance time (PCT);
(c) buffer start ≤ start of red clearance interval, if a red clearance interval is used.

Figure 4I-4 note (11th Ed.) reinforces that the buffer is not optional: "The Buffer Interval, which shall always be provided and displayed, may be used to help satisfy the calculated pedestrian clearance time, or may begin after the calculated pedestrian clearance time has ended." The same figure shows the permitted relationships to the concurrent vehicular phase: Yellow Change Interval = Buffer Interval, or Yellow Change Interval + Red Clearance Interval = Buffer Interval. In ordinary operation the 2 s floor is therefore usually exceeded incidentally, because the buffer typically spans a 3 s or longer yellow plus red clearance.

3. WALKING SPEED — WHAT "DEFAULT" MEANS

The 11th Edition fixes 3.5 ft/s as the speed the pedestrian clearance time is sized for unless a documented reason exists to go slower. §4I.06 ¶10 (Guidance) reads verbatim:

"Where pedestrians who walk slower than 3.5 feet per second, or pedestrians who use wheelchairs, routinely use the crosswalk, a walking speed of less than 3.5 feet per second should be considered in determining the pedestrian clearance time."

Engineering reading: 3.5 ft/s is the default/nominal design speed; it is a ceiling on the design speed, not a floor. The adjustment is one-directional — you may and often should go slower (common practice: 3.0 ft/s at schools, senior centers, hospitals, transit stations, APS-equipped crossings in such areas), never faster. 3.5 ft/s is unchanged from the 2009 MUTCD, so this is not a source of discrepancy between editions.

4. 2009 MUTCD COMPARISON (ask 3)

MUTCD 2009, §4E.06 "Pedestrian Intervals and Signal Phases," ¶3 (Standard), contained the parallel provision:

"Following the pedestrian change interval, a buffer interval consisting of a steady UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall be displayed for at least 3 seconds prior to the release of any conflicting vehicular movement."

Context that matters for a reviewer: the buffer interval as a named requirement was introduced by the 2009 MUTCD (the 2003 MUTCD had no buffer-interval requirement; it relied on the pedestrian change interval plus the vehicular change/clearance intervals). The 11th Edition retained the mechanism, lowered the numeric floor to 2 s, and strengthened the obligation to display the buffer in every pedestrian phase.

Note on evidence: the 2009 quotation above is reproduced from the published 2009 MUTCD text from professional knowledge — the fetched source set for this task did not include the 2009 edition. It is a one-lookup verification: 2009 MUTCD PDF (mutcd.fhwa.dot.gov/pdfs/2009r1r2/), Part 4, Chapter 4E, §4E.06, ¶3. The 11th Edition values (2 s; 3.5 ft/s) are directly supported by the fetched primary text.

5. HOW TO APPLY IT — CONTROLLER TIMING PROCEDURE

Step 1. Compute PCT = crossing distance (ft, curb to far curb or to a refuge median of adequate width) ÷ walking speed (ft/s). Use 3.5 ft/s by default; use a lower value where warranted per ¶10, and document the justification in the timing sheet.
Step 2. Assign the walk interval: 7 s guidance minimum, 4 s permitted option where pedestrian volumes/characteristics allow (§4I.06 ¶¶11–12).
Step 3. Set buffer = 2 s minimum. Set pedestrian change interval (flashing DONT WALK) ≥ PCT − buffer.
Step 4. Verify constraint (a): the conflicting vehicular movement's green must not start until the buffer has been displayed for ≥ 2 s. Verify (b): flashing + buffer ≥ PCT. Verify (c): buffer start ≤ red clearance start.
Step 5. Round upward to the controller's whole-second resolution; never round a minimum down.

Worked example (check arithmetic against the constraints above):
• Crosswalk length 60 ft, default speed 3.5 ft/s → PCT = 60 ÷ 3.5 = 17.14 s.
• Buffer = 2.0 s (minimum).
• Flashing DONT WALK ≥ 17.14 − 2.0 = 15.14 s → program 15.2 s (or 16 s at whole-second resolution).
• Check (b): 15.2 + 2.0 = 17.2 s ≥ 17.14 s ✓. Check (a): buffer 2.0 s ≥ 2.0 s ✓.
• Total pedestrian phase = walk 7.0 + flashing 15.2 + buffer 2.0 = 24.2 s; the concurrent through movement's yellow + red clearance must be long enough that the buffer does not delay the release beyond the intended coordination offset — if it does, lengthen the flashing interval, not shorten the buffer.

6. QA / REVIEW CHECKLIST

• Is the buffer ≥ 2 s and does it terminate at or before the conflicting green? (11th Ed. floor)
• Is flashing + buffer ≥ PCT computed at 3.5 ft/s or a documented slower speed?
• Is a slower speed used where the crossing serves a hospital, school, senior housing, transit stop, or APS-equipped crossing with high older-adult/wheelchair use? If not, is the omission justified in writing?
• Does the buffer start no later than the red clearance start?
• Are legacy 3 s buffers being retained? That is compliant — 3 s ≥ 2 s. There is no need to retime to shorten a 3 s buffer, and doing so would consume the safety margin the 2009 standard provided.
• If a local/state supplement is in force, check it: several state supplements restate §4I.06 with the same 2 s floor (e.g., the Ohio supplement to the 11th Ed. reproduces ¶04 with 'at least 2 seconds'), but supplements can be more restrictive and govern where they are.

7. SCOPE AND ASSUMPTIONS

• Edition: 11th Edition, December 2023, with Revision 1 (December 2025) incorporated. The fetched Revision 1 sources reproduce §4I.06 ¶04 with the 2 s minimum, so the Revision 1 text does not change the answer.
• Scope is standard signalized/midblock pedestrian crossings. Exclusive pedestrian phases, leading pedestrian intervals, PHBs (Part 4J), and APS timing adjustments do not alter the 2 s buffer floor or the 3.5 ft/s default; they add requirements on top of them.
• Countdown-related guidance (§4I.04 ¶07) — flashing set to approximately 4 s less than the required PCT with an additional steady-DONT-WALK clearance interval where there is no concurrent vehicular phase — is a separate provision and does not modify the 2 s minimum in §4I.06.
• Out of my function as Traffic Engineer: this answer does not opine on legal liability, on whether a jurisdiction must retroactively retime existing signals (the MUTCD minimum is a floor; existing 3 s buffers already comply), or on the FHWA rulemaking rationale beyond noting the numeric change.

verdict.summary:
# SPCC Applicability — Two Capacity Ceilings and the Aboveground Counting Rule

Scope: a U.S. onshore industrial facility that is non-transportation-related (not a vessel, not a pipeline) and stores oil in aboveground drums and tanks plus some completely buried tanks. The question is regulatory-text applicability, not a facility inventory; no container capacities were supplied, so the deliverable is the rule plus a counting procedure a engineer can apply directly.

## 1. The two cealings (ask 1, 2, 3)

| # | Storage category | Ceiling — must stay AT OR UNDER | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Aggregated aboveground storage capacity | **1,320 U.S. gallons of oil** | 40 CFR 112.1(f)(2)(ii) |
| 2 | Completely buried storage capacity | **42,000 U.S. gallons of oil** | 40 CFR 112.1(f)(2)(i) |

Both must hold. 112.1(f)(2) exempts a facility only if it 'meets both of the following requirements' — (i) buried ≤42,000 and (ii) aboveground ≤1,320. Exceeding either one alone puts the facility inside Part 112, irrespective of the other.

Boundary semantics (ask 3). The rule's own words are '…or less', and EPA's applicability flowchart asks whether the total is 'greater than 1,320' / 'greater than 42,000'. Therefore exactly 1,320 gal and exactly 42,000 gal are OUTSIDE coverage; 1,321 and 42,001 are inside. Two practical consequences: (i) the comparison is against capacity, not against oil on hand, so a drum that is empty but not permanently closed still counts; (ii) a facility sitting exactly at a cealing has zero headroom — one additional 55-gal drum takes it inside — so operate with margin and re-run the calculation on any change.

Beating both cealings is necessary but not sufficient for non-coverage. The other applicability tests still apply: the facility must be non-transportation-related, must be engaged in drilling, producing, gathering, storing, processing, refinning, transferring, distributing, using, or consuming oil, and must not be able to reasonably be expected to discharge oil in quantities that may be harmful into navigable waters or adjoining shorelines. If those are met and either cealing is exceeded, a SPCC Plan is required under 112.3.

## 2. Which aboveground containers count toward the 1,320 (ask 4)

A container is counted toward the aboveground total when ALL of the following hold:

1. **It is an aboveground container, or is treated as one.** The container-inclusion list in 112.1 (the paragraph immediately preceding (c); cited in secondary references as 112.1(b)) provides that any 'bunkered tank' or 'partially buried tank' as defined in 112.2, or any container in a vault, is each considered an aboveground storage container for purposes of Part 112. Completely buried tanks are NOT in this total (they go to the 42,000 side).
2. **Its storage capacity is 55 U.S. gallons or greater.** 112.1(f)(2)(ii): 'only containers with a capacity of 55 U.S. gallons or greater are counted'; 112.1(f)(5) separately exempts 'any container with a storage capacity of less than 55 gallons of oil'. 55 gal exactly counts; 54.9 gal does not.
3. **It is counted at full nameplate capacity**, regardless of how full it is. The inclusion list expressly covers any container 'used for standby storage, for seasonal storage, or for temporary storage, or not otherwise permanently closed' — so idle, empty, or half-full drums and tanks count unless they meet the 112.2 definition of 'permanently closed'.
4. **It is not on the exclusion list** below.

### Excluded from the aboveground total
Per 112.1(f)(2)(ii)(A)-(F) and the parallel exemptions in 112.1(f)(5)-(12):

- **(A)** The capacity of a container that is 'permanently closed' as defined in 112.2 (emptied of oil, vented, and rendered inoperable by removing and capping all connecting pipes — and recorded/marked as such). An empty drum that has NOT been rendered permanently closed still counts.
- **(B)/(7)** Motive power containers as defined in 112.2 — containers that supply fuel to an engine that propels a motor vehicle, motor vehicle, or vessel (vehicle fuel tanks, locomotive/aircraft tanks). Caveat: 112.1(f)(7) states that the transfer of fuel or other oil into a motive power container at an otherwise regulated facility does not inherit this exclusion.
- **(C)/(8)** Hot-mix asphalt, or any hot-mix asphalt container.
- **(D)/(9)** Any container for heating oil used solely at a single-family residence.
- **(E)/(10)** Pesticide application equipment and related mix containers.
- **(F)/(12)** Any milk and milk product container and associated piping and appurtenances.
- **Containers under 55 gal** (112.1(f)(5)).
- **Storage containers used exclusively for wastewater treatment.** EPA's applicability guidance instructs 'Do not include … storage containers used exclusively for wastewater treatment'; the reguly structure rests on 112.1(f)(6) (any facility or part thereof used exclusively for wastewater treatment and not used to satisfy any requirement of Part 112), with the caveat that 'the production, recovery, or recycling of oil is not wastewater treatment'.
- **(Not containers, but commonly miscounted)** Intra-facility gathering lines subject to 49 CFR 192 or 195 (112.1(f)(11)) — piping volume is not part of any container total.

### Drums specifically
A 55-gal drum counts in full (55 gal); a 30-gal drum, 5-gal pail, or 1-gal can does not. Intermediate bulk containers (e.g., 275-gal IBCs/totes) count in full. Twenty-four 55-gal drums alone equal 1,320 gal — i.e., a drum farm can reach the cealing with no tank at all.

## 3. Which buried tanks count toward the 42,000

**Counted:** 'completely buried tanks' as defined in 112.2 — tanks that are completely buried and are not aboveground, bunkered, or partially buried (those three go to the aboveground side).

**Excluded** from the completely buried storage capacity (112.1(f)(2)(i); EPA's applicability page states the same list):
- Completely buried tanks subject to ALL of the technical requirements of 40 CFR 280 or 281. Note 'all' — a tank deferred from, or excluded from, any 280 technical requirement does not qualify for this exclusion and its capacity counts.
- Containers with a storage capacity of less than 55 gal.
- Permanently closed containers.
- Containers used exclusively for wastewater treatment.

**Bburied piping is not counted:** the category is 'completely buried tank', not piping; buried piping volume does not enter the 42,000 sum (though it is a potential discharge source and belongs in the facility diagram if the facility is regulated).

## 4. Procedure to apply at the facility

1. **Define the facility boundary.** Aggregate every container under common ownership at the contiguous site; do not split a site into convenient sub-areas to stay under a cealing.
2. **Inventory every container** that holds or is intended to hold oil: nameplate capacity (gal), location class (aboveground / bunkered / partially buried / in a vault / completely buried), status (in service, standby, seasonal, temporary, permanently closed), and exclusion basis if any.
3. **Compute A** = Σ capacity of aboveground-class containers with capacity ≥55 gal, less the exclusions in §2.
4. **Compute B** = Σ capacity of completely buried tanks with capacity ≥55 gal, less 280/281-regulated tanks and the other exclusions in §3.
5. **Compare:** outside coverage on capacity grounds if **A ≤ 1,320 AND B ≤ 42,000**; inside if **A > 1,320 OR B > 42,000**. Then confirm the non-transportation / oil-handling / reasonable-potential-to-discharge tests.
6. **Document** the container list, the arithmetic, and the definitional basis for each exclusion — this is the audit trail, and it becomes the basis of the facility diagram and Plan if the facility is regulated.
7. **Re-run** whenever a container is added, replaced, returned to service, or reclassified (e.g., a 'permanently closed' drum put back in service).

### Worked illustration (hypothetical — arithmetic demonstration only; no facility data were supplied)
- 12 × 55-gal drums (660) + 1,000-gal aboveground tank (1,000) + 500-gal partially buried tank (500, counted as aboveground) → A = 2,160 gal > 1,320 → **inside** Part 112 on the aboveground test alone, whatever B is.
- Remove the partially buried tank and reduce to 6 drums → 330 + 1,000 = 1,330 > 1,320 → still **inside**.
- Reduce to 5 drums → 275 + 1,000 = 1,275 ≤ 1,320 → **outside** on the aboveground test, provided B ≤ 42,000 gal and the other applicability tests are not met.

## 5. What this determination does NOT decide (avoid misapplying the numbers)

- **Substantial-harm / Facility Response Plan.** Appendix F uses different figures and different tests — 'total oil storage capacity ≥42,000 gallons' where operations include over-water transfers of oil to or from vessels, and '≥1 million gallons' with inadequate secondary containment. The 42,000 figure appears there in a different role; it is not a second applicability cealing.
- **Qualified Facility status.** The 10,000-gal total-capacity line in 112.6 governs self-certification of a Plan, not whether a Plan is needed.
- **Other programs.** State and local oil-storage rules, CWA §311(j) authority, the UST rules (40 CFR 280/281), and state-administered SPCC programs can apply below these cealings. The federal SPCC applicability cealings are a floor, not a safe harbor.
- **Unresolved by the quoted text — decide conservatively and document:** (i) oil-filled operational equipment (transformeres, hydralic power units, machining coolent reservoirs) — whether these are 'containers' at all; (ii) fuel tanks mounted on vehicles or trailers used exclusively on site (motive-power exclusion vs. counting); (iii) multiple non-contiguous parcels under one owner (one facility or several).

## 6. Citation note

Ceilings and exclusions are quoted from 40 CFR 112.1 as currently published (eCFR, fetched 2026-11-23) and from the CFR-2024 title 40 vol 24 PDF of 112.1; the boundary and the buried-side exclusion list are confirmed against EPA's applicability page ('Does the SPCC Rule Apply to Your Facility?', fetched 2026-11-23). The factors for derived units not included in Secs. B.8 and B.9 can readily be found from the factors given.
Examples:
To find the factor for converting values in lb · ft/s to values in kg · m/s, obtain from Sec. B.8 or B.9
1 lb = 4.535 924 E-01 kg
1 ft = 3.048 E-01 m
and substitute these values into the unit lb · ft/s to obtain

verdict.summary:
CHILLER CAPACITY CONVERSION — 10 TON (US) OF REFRIGERATION TO kW

ANSWER
  10 tons of refrigeration = 35.17 kW (four significant figures).
  Unrounded: 35.168 53 kW.

1. CONVERSION FACTOR USED (NIST, official)

Source: NIST Special Publication 811, Guide for the Use of the International System of Units (SI), Appendix B.9, table "Heat Flow Rate". Entry, quoted as published:

    ton of refrigeration (12 000 Btu_IT/h)  →  watt (W)  →  3.516 853 E+03

Therefore, exactly as NIST publishes it:

    1 ton of refrigeration = 3 516.853 W = 3.516 853 kW

This is the definitional entry NIST gives for the ton of refrigeration, keyed explicitly to the International Table Btu (Btu_IT) at 12 000 Btu_IT/h. No secondary or rounded source (e.g. the commonly quoted 3.517 kW/ton) is used.

2. INDEPENDENT CROSS-CHECK OF THE FACTOR FROM NIST'S OWN Btu_IT/h ENTRY

Same SP 811 Appendix B.9 table (Heat Flow Rate):

    1 Btu_IT/h = 2.930 711 E-01 W

    12 000 Btu_IT/h × 0.293 071 1 W/(Btu_IT/h) = 3 516.853 2 W = 3.516 853 kW

This reproduces the tabulated ton-of-refrigeration factor to all seven published digits, confirming the factor is the IT-Btu basis and that no transcription error has been introduced.

3. CALCULATION

    Q = 10 TR × 3.516 853 kW/TR = 35.168 53 kW

Rounding to four significant figures:

    digits: 3, 5, 1, 6 | next digit 8 → round the 6 up

    Q = 35.17 kW   (4 s.f.)

Rounding error introduced: 35.17 − 35.168 53 = 0.001 47 kW, i.e. 0.004 % — well inside the 4-significant-figure resolution of 0.01 kW.

4. EQUIVALENT EXPRESSIONS (same quantity, for the equipment schedule)

    Cooling capacity        = 35.17 kW
                            = 35 168.53 W
                            = 120 000 Btu_IT/h  (nameplate basis, 10 × 12 000)
                            = 10.0 ton of refrigeration (US)
                            = 126.6 MJ/h
                            = 35.17 kJ/s
    Specific basis          = 3.517 kW/TR (rounded check: 35.17 / 10 = 3.517)

5. WHY THE IT-Btu MATTERS AT THE FOURTH SIGNIFICANT FIGURE

The ton of refrigeration is a definition (12 000 Btu/h); the Btu is not single-valued. Using NIST's thermochemical-Btu entry instead (1 Btu_th/h = 2.928 751 E-01 W):

    12 000 × 0.292 875 1 = 3 514.50 W → 10 TR = 35.145 kW → 35.15 kW (4 s.f.)

The IT and thermochemical answers differ by 0.07 %, which is visible in the fourth significant figure (35.17 vs 35.15). The request specifies the IT definition and NIST's tabulated ton-of-refrigeration factor, so 35.17 kW is the correct figure; 35.15 kW is recorded here only as the sensitivity that the fourth digit exposes. (NIST's other Btu entries — mean, 39 °F, 59 °F, 60 °F — are likewise not applicable.)

6. ENGINEERING NOTES ON THE RESULT (HVAC context)

  - 35.17 kW is the chiller's *cooling* (thermal) capacity — the rate of heat removed at the evaporator. It is not the electrical input. It is the number to use for load matching, air/water-side ΔT and flow sizing, and pipe/duct sizing.
  - Electrical draw is a separate figure obtained from the unit's kW/ton or COP at rated conditions. For illustration only, a water-cooled chiller at about 0.6 kW/ton would draw roughly 6 kW at this capacity; a small air-cooled package would be nearer 1.0–1.2 kW/ton, roughly 10–12 kW. These are typical values, not this unit's rating — take the actual figure from the nameplate or rating sheet.
  - The nameplate "ton" on a US-manufactured chiller is the US ton of refrigeration (12 000 Btu_IT/h, i.e. the heat to melt 2 000 lb of ice in 24 h). It is not a ton of mass and not a metric ton of refrigeration; do not substitute short-ton mass or metric-tonne conventions.
  - Presentation: state as 35.17 kW (4 s.f.). Reporting 35.2 kW would be three significant figures and 35.169 kW would overstate the precision of a nameplate rating.

7. ONE-LINE AUDIT TRAIL

    10 TR × (12 000 Btu_IT/h per TR) × (0.293 071 1 W per Btu_IT/h) ÷ 1 000 W/kW
      = 10 × 3.516 853 kW = 35.168 53 kW → 35.17 kW
    Factor source: NIST SP 811, Appendix B.9, "ton of refrigeration (12 000 Btu_IT/h) = 3.516 853 E+03 W".

1.1.7 AVCC
AVCC is the supply voltage pin for the A/D Converter, PC3:0, and ADC7:6. It should be externally connected to

In the TQFP and QFN/MLF package, ADC7:6 serve as analog inputs to the A/D converter. These pins are

2. Overview
The ATmega48A/PA/88A/PA/168A/PA/328/P is a low-power CMOS 8-bit microcontroller based on the AVR
enhanced RISC architecture. By executing powerful instructions in a single clock cycle, the
ATmega48A/PA/88A/PA/168A/PA/328/P achieves throughputs approaching 1 MIPS per MHz allowing the
system designer to optimize power consumption versus processing speed.

Hardware Engineering Gotchas
Real-world hardware caveats, PCB layout constraints and silicon errata to know before manufacturing.
Critical
Combined Package and Port Group Current Limits
The 40 mA per-pin absolute maximum is a stress limit, not a guaranteed drive capability (output voltage is characterized at 20 mA and VCC = 5 V under the stated temperature conditions); total current through all VCC and GND pins must not exceed 200 mA. Additionally, Microchip enforces strict port group current limits: total steady-state sink current (IOL) must not exceed 100 mA each for (1) Ports C0-C5 + ADC6/ADC7, (2) Ports B0-B5 + D5-D7 + XTAL1/XTAL2, and (3) Ports D0-D4 + RESET. Total source current (IOH) must not exceed 150 mA each for (1) Ports C0-C5 + D0-D4 + ADC7 + RESET, and (2) Ports B0-B5 + D5-D7 + ADC6 + XTAL1/XTAL2.

verdict.summary:
# ATmega328P in 28-pin PDIP — thermal ratings in Microchip DS40002061B (09/2020)

## 0. Bottom line

**Ask 2 — junction-to-ambient thermal resistance: NOT SPECIFIED in this datasheet.** DS40002061B contains no thermal-resistance data of any kind for the ATmega328P — no theta-JA, no theta-JC, no psi-JT, no thermal-resistance-vs-airflow table, no derating curve, no 'Thermal Considerations' section — for the 28-lead PDIP (package code 28P3) or for any of the other three packages in the family (32A TQFP, 28M1 QFN, 32M1-A QFN). The figure does not exist in the cited document; it is not a hard-to-find table. Reported as blocked rather than answered with a number that cannot be traced to the source.

**Ask 3 — maximum junction temperature / total power dissipation: NOT SPECIFIED.** The datasheet states neither a Tj(max) nor a Ptot (total power dissipation) rating. The only thermal and current limits it does state are given in §1 below. The -55 degC to +125 degC figure in the Absolute Maximum Ratings is an operating (ambient) temperature range for the part, not a junction-temperature rating; the datasheet never uses 'junction temperature' as a limiting parameter.

Anyone quoting e.g. '45 degC/W' or '1 W at 25 degC' as an ATmega328P datasheet value is quoting a different document — a Microchip package thermal-data table, a JEDEC JESD51 report, a distributor page, or another AVR family (e.g. ATmega8/ATmega16-era datasheets, which did carry power-dissipation rows).

## 1. What DS40002061B actually specifies (the limits that do exist)

**§29.1 Absolute Maximum Ratings (ATmega328P electrical characteristics chapter, p. 308 in the 09/2020 printing — section number is stable, page numbers can shift by a page between printings):**

- Operating temperature: -55 degC to +125 degC
- Storage temperature: -65 degC to +150 degC
- Voltage on any pin except RESET with respect to ground: -0.5 V to VCC + 0.5 V
- Voltage on RESET with respect to ground: -0.5 V to +13.0 V
- Maximum operating voltage: 6.0 V
- DC current, VCC and GND pins: 200.0 mA
- DC current, any I/O pin: 40.0 mA
- DC current, RESET pin: 40.0 mA
- DC current, AVCC pin: 40.0 mA

Note the absence of any row containing the words 'thermal', 'junction', 'dissipation' or a theta symbol. The section carries the usual stress caveat that exposure to absolute-maximum conditions for extended periods may affect reliability.

**§29.2 DC Characteristics:** guaranteed over TA = -40 degC to +85 degC (industrial). The ordering table (p. 627) additionally lists -AN/-ANR and -PN/-PNR ordering codes specified over -40 degC to +105 degC.

**§29.3 Speed Grades:** 0-4 MHz @ 1.8-5.5 V, 0-10 MHz @ 2.7-5.5 V, 0-20 MHz @ 4.5-5.5 V.

**Ordering/package identification (p. 627):** ATmega328P-PU / -PN = package code 28P3 = '28-lead, 0.300 in Wide, Plastic Dual Inline Package (PDIP)'.

## 2. Rulings per ask

| Ask | Question | Ruling | Basis in DS40002061B |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | theta-JA of ATmega328P, 28-pin PDIP, degC/W | Not specified — no such parameter in the document | §29.1 and the whole electrical-characteristics chapter contain no thermal-resistance data; §39 (Packaging Information, 32A / 28M1 / 32M1-A / 28P3 drawings) is mechanical only |
| 3 | Maximum junction temperature or total power dissipation specified | Not specified — neither parameter is rated | §29.1 lists an operating-temperature range of -55 to +125 degC and current ceilings (200 mA VCC/GND, 40 mA per I/O, 40 mA RESET, 40 mA AVCC); no Tj row, no Ptot row |

**Warning on secondary sources.** One third-party page in circulation (CircuitBase, 'ATmega328P-PU') renders the Absolute Maximum Ratings row 'Operating temperature -55 degC to +125 degC' as 'Junction temperature -55 to 125 degC'. That is a re-labelling, not a datasheet rating. Do not carry it into a thermal analysis or a design review document as Tj(max).

## 3. If a theta-JA number is genuinely required — procedure

1. **Ask Microchip for it against the package code.** The correct request is for the thermal characteristics of package code 28P3 (28-lead, 0.300 in PDIP), not for the ATmega328P specifically — thermal resistance is a package property, so the same value applies to every device in a 28P3. Microchip publishes package thermal data separately from device datasheets (packaging specification pages and support-issued thermal data). Cite the package code in the request; a device-name request usually returns the datasheet you already have.
2. **If Microchip cannot supply it, measure or model it.** The governing standards are JEDEC JESD51-2 (still air), JESD51-3 (low-effective-thermal-conductivity test board) and JESD51-7 (high-effective-thermal-conductivity test board). A theta-JA quoted without its board and airflow condition is not usable for a design decision.
3. **If neither is available, use a labelled industry-typical value with margin.** For a 28-lead, 0.300 in PDIP in still air: theta-JA is typically in the 45-60 degC/W range on a JEDEC 2-layer board, falling toward 35-45 degC/W with a 4-layer board and copper spreading at the leads; theta-JC is typically 15-20 degC/W. **These are INDUSTRY-TYPICAL figures for the package family, not ATmega328P datasheet values.** Use the worst case (60 degC/W) and carry the label into any document you produce.
4. **Treat the result as a sanity check, not a qualification.** For this device the thermal path is the package leads only — a PDIP has no thermal pad and no exposed die pad. A socket adds contact resistance and a small thermal penalty; long unsupported leads in a socketed assembly are the dominant variability.

## 4. Worked thermal budget (DERIVED — not datasheet values)

Model: TJ = TA + theta-JA x P_D, with TJ held at the §29.1 absolute-maximum operating temperature of 125 degC purely as a stress ceiling (not a design target), and P_D capped by the §29.1 current limit of 200 mA through VCC/GND at 5.5 V = **1.10 W**.

| Assumed theta-JA (degC/W) | P_D ceiling at TA = 25 degC | P_D ceiling at TA = 85 degC | P_D ceiling at TA = 105 degC |
|---|---|---|---|
| 45 | 1.10 W (current limit binds; thermal would allow 2.22 W) | 0.89 W | 0.44 W |
| 50 | 1.10 W (current limit binds; thermal would allow 2.00 W) | 0.80 W | 0.40 W |
| 60 | 1.10 W (current limit binds; thermal would allow 1.67 W) | 0.67 W | 0.33 W |

Reading of the table: at room ambient the 200 mA current ceiling binds before the thermal ceiling; at high ambient the thermal budget binds first. Both ceilings are derived, neither is a datasheet rating.

**Reality check against actual device dissipation.** A normally operating ATmega328P at full clock and 5.5 V draws well under 20 mA (see the Icc rows in §29.2), i.e. under 110 mW; at 50 degC/W that is a junction rise of about 5.5 degC. A 100 mW device in an 85 degC ambient sits at roughly TJ = 90 degC. **Conclusion for design: thermal resistance is not a limiting factor for a normally operating ATmega328P in the 28P3 PDIP.** The binding constraints in practice are the 200 mA total VCC/GND current limit, the 40 mA per-pin limit, the port-group current limits, and TA <= 85 degC (or <= 105 degC for -PN/-AN).

**Design targets to use in the absence of a datasheet Tj rating:** keep TJ below about 100-105 degC at worst-case ambient and worst-case dissipation (a conventional 20 degC derating below the 125 degC stress ceiling), and never treat 125 degC as an operating target. If the application is near the 0.3-0.8 W region implied above, the PDIP is the wrong package — move to the 32M1-A QFN, which has a exposed pad and a far lower theta-JA.

**On-die temperature sensing (for trend only).** The ATmega328P has an internal temperature sensor on ADC8 (MUX = 1000b, §24.9 'Temperature Measurement'). Its absolute accuracy is about plus/minus 10 degC and it is uncalibrated, so it is usable for relative trending and for detecting self-heating, not for verifying an absolute TJ. Do not use it to close a thermal budget.

## 5. Number register (so datasheet, derived and typical values are never mixed)

| Number | Meaning | Status |
|---|---|---|
| -55 degC to +125 degC | Absolute-maximum operating temperature | DATASHEET, §29.1 |
| -65 degC to +150 degC | Storage temperature | DATASHEET, §29.1 |
| 200 mA | DC current, VCC and GND pins | DATASHEET, §29.1 |
| 40 mA | DC current, per I/O pin / RESET / AVCC | DATASHEET, §29.1 |
| 6.0 V | Maximum operating voltage | DATASHEET, §29.1 |
| -40 to +85 degC / -40 to +105 degC | Guaranteed operating ambient (industrial / -AN,-PN codes) | DATASHEET, §29.2 and ordering table p. 627 |
| 1.10 W | 200 mA x 5.5 V current-limit-derived dissipation ceiling | DERIVED |
| 45-60 degC/W, 15-20 degC/W | theta-JA (still air, JEDEC 2-layer) and theta-JC, 28-lead 0.300 in PDIP | INDUSTRY-TYPICAL, not ATmega328P datasheet |
| 0.33-0.89 W, 0.40-2.22 W | Thermal-budget dissipation ceilings in the table in §4 | DERIVED from the assumed theta-JA above |

## 6. Verification checklist (about five minutes, against the actual PDF)

1. Open DS40002061B and go to the ATmega328P electrical-characteristics chapter, §29.1 'Absolute Maximum Ratings' (p. 308 in the 09/2020 printing).
2. Confirm the bulleted list matches §1 above, and confirm there is no row containing 'thermal', 'junction', 'dissipation' or a theta symbol.
3. Full-document search for 'thermal', 'theta', 'junction', 'dissipation'. Expect hits only on the typical-characteristic graphs (temperature-labelled curves) and the ordering/package pages — no ratings table.
4. Confirm package code 28P3 = 28-lead, 0.300 in PDIP in the ordering table (p. 627) and that §39 contains only mechanical drawings for 32A, 28M1, 32M1-A and 28P3.
5. If a customer or QA record requires a theta-JA, raise the request against package code 28P3 as described in §3 rather than back-filling a number from a secondary source.

## 7. Direct answers as they should be recorded

- Ask 2 (theta-JA, ATmega328P, 28-pin PDIP, DS40002061B 09/2020): **not specified in the datasheet.** No value exists in the cited source; blocked.
- Ask 3 (maximum junction temperature or total power dissipation specified by the datasheet): **none specified.** The nearest stated limits are the absolute-maximum operating temperature of -55 degC to +125 degC, the guaranteed operating ambient of -40 to +85 degC (-40 to +105 degC for -AN/-PN), and the 200 mA / 40 mA current ceilings of §29.1.
